title: Bury the coins before you sweep
allegory: Algorithmic-task interpretability is like testing a metal detector on a patch of beach where you buried the coins yourself: because you know where every coin is, you can see which ones it finds, which it misses and where it beeps at bare sand, before you trust it on a beach you can't dig up.
map: a task whose correct algorithm you know in advance: balanced brackets
your interpretability method: logit attribution, ablation, causal scrubbing
recovering the right parts: head 2.0 checks the count, head 2.1 checks the dip
coins missed and beeps over bare sand
the gap: the combined story recovered only about 72% of the loss
only then sweeping a beach you can't dig up
trusting the method on real models with no ground truth

props.label: a neat story about the model

cap.1: Your interpretability tool tells a neat story about what a model is doing. On a big model there's no answer sheet. How would you ever know it's right?
cap.2: In real LLMs the true mechanism is unknown, so a plausible explanation and a correct one look identical. You need a test bench where the right answer is known in advance.
cap.3: Methods can produce compelling but unfaithful explanations. Tasks with a known solution act as calibration: they show what a method recovers, misses and invents.

props.label: map of where you buried them

cap.1: Test a metal detector where you buried the coins yourself. You know every spot, so you can see what it finds, what it misses, and where it beeps at nothing.
cap.2: Train a tiny model on a task whose algorithm you already know, reverse-engineer it with your tools, and grade the explanation against the answer you wrote down first.
cap.3: Known-ground-truth tasks such as bracket balancing, modular addition and Othello turn interpretability from storytelling into something you can score.

chapters.name: The answer sheet
chapters.title: walk right to left: a close adds 1, an open takes 1

cap.1: The answer sheet: walk right to left, add one for a close bracket, take one for an open. Balanced means you never dip below zero and finish at exactly zero.
cap.2: Exercise: hand-write is_balanced with a for loop. It fails in two ways: the count doesn't end at zero, or the running count goes negative somewhere. Those two clauses are what you hunt for.
cap.3: Ground-truth predicates: total_elevation_failure (unequal opens and closes) and negative_failure (the elevation dips below zero, an open never closed). They label every eval string by failure type.

cap.1: Work backwards from the model's 'unbalanced' verdict. Two heads in the last layer do most of the pushing, and each owns one of the two checks.
cap.2: Logit attribution run backwards: push the unbalanced-minus-balanced direction back through ln_final and split the residual stream by component. Heads 2.0 and 2.1 dominate: 2.0 the total, 2.1 the dip.
cap.3: Freeze ln_final's observed per-sequence scale before projecting, or the components won't sum to the logit. Head 2.0's output is close to affine in the fraction of open brackets.

chapters.name: Only 72% explained
chapters.title: loss recovered by the whole two-heads story under causal scrubbing

cap.1: Redwood tested the neat two-heads story by scrambling everything it called irrelevant. Only about 72% of the model's performance survived. The story was incomplete.
cap.2: Causal scrubbing resamples every activation the hypothesis calls unimportant from other inputs and measures loss recovered. Each claim alone scored high; all together, about 72%.
cap.3: Chan et al. (Redwood, 2022): head 2.0 caught unbalanced strings the count test doesn't explain, and 2.1 missed some failures it should own. Log-loss rewards both heads voting together, so the split is leaky.

props.label: a string built to fool it

cap.1: The real test of understanding: use it to build a string that fools the model. If your story is right, you can predict where the model breaks.
cap.2: Head 2.0's signal is close to a straight line in the fraction of open brackets. That lets you invert the mechanism and hand-build strings the model confidently misclassifies.
cap.3: Adversarial construction is a falsifiable check: an explanation that predicts new failures is doing more than fitting attributions after the fact.

cap.1: Before pointing interpretability at models we can't check, prove the tools on ones we can. That's how we learn which stories about AI deserve trust.
cap.2: Even on a three-layer model with a known answer, a careful story explained about 72%. Expect gaps on real models, and prefer methods that report how much they explain.
cap.3: Known-ground-truth tasks (brackets, modular addition, Othello) are the calibration set of interpretability: they separate the method's error from the model's complexity.

readouts.label: check 1, head 2.0's job: ends at zero?
check 2, head 2.1's job: never below zero?
readouts.f: G[0].slice().reverse().reduce((acc, v) => acc.concat([(acc.length ? acc[acc.length - 1] : 0) + (v ? 1 : -1)]), []).reduce((m, e) => e < m ? e : m, 0) >= 0 ? 'pass' : 'fail: it dips below zero'

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: sum(G[0].map(v => v ? 1 : -1)) == 0 && G[0].slice().reverse().reduce((acc, v) => acc.concat([(acc.length ? acc[acc.length - 1] : 0) + (v ? 1 : -1)]), []).reduce((m, e) => e < m ? e : m, 0) >= 0 ? 'balanced' : 'unbalanced'

caption.1: Click cells to flip brackets: 0 is '(' and 1 is ')'. Watch both checks. Can you build a string with equal counts that still fails?
caption.2: These are the two clauses of the ground-truth algorithm, the ones heads 2.0 and 2.1 split between them. ') ( ) (' has equal counts yet fails check 2: scanning from the right, an open is never closed.
caption.3: ARENA computes elevation right to left and reads the classification from position 0 of a bidirectional model. Knowing the target predicates exactly is what lets you grade an attribution against the truth.

where_else: Grokking: a one-layer model on modular addition, fully reverse-engineered as a Fourier algorithm and then used to build progress measures
OthelloGPT: a model trained on legal moves, whose board state turned out to be linear once probed as mine versus theirs
Causal scrubbing and other faithfulness tests, which score any circuit story by how much of the loss it recovers
Planted-bug testing in software: seed known faults to measure what a checker catches before you trust it

hamming.what: Reverse-engineering a tiny model trained on a task whose correct algorithm you already know, so you can grade what your interpretability method recovers.
hamming.when: Before trusting a technique on real models, and whenever a new method needs a benchmark: brackets, modular addition, Othello.
hamming.why: Without ground truth a plausible explanation and a correct one look the same; a known answer shows what a method finds, misses and invents.

object.title: The bracket checker's wiring
object.subtitle: Three layers, two heads each: the two last-layer heads that carry the verdict, and the part of the model the neat story left out.

nodes.label: extra layer 1 logic, not in the story

cap.1: The whole bracket checker: three layers with two heads each. Brackets come in on the left; the verdict, balanced or not, comes out on the right.
cap.2: A three-layer, two-heads-per-layer bidirectional transformer trained to classify bracket strings up to 40 tokens long, read out at position 0.
cap.3: No causal mask: every position attends to every other, and padding must be masked by a permanent hook or position 0 absorbs contributions from padding.

cap.1: Working backwards from the verdict, two heads in the last layer carry most of the push: 2.0 and 2.1.
cap.2: Direct logit attribution along the unbalanced-minus-balanced direction, with ln_final's scale frozen, ranks heads 2.0 and 2.1 far above the rest.
cap.3: Decomposed contributions only sum to the true logit difference once each is scaled by the observed ln_final.hook_scale; assert the sum before trusting the ranking.

cap.1: Each owns one clause of the answer sheet: 2.0 checks the count ends at zero, 2.1 checks it never dips below zero along the way.
cap.2: Split the eval set by failure type and scatter each head's output: 2.0 lines up with total-count failures, 2.1 with dips below zero.
cap.3: Conditioning on total_elevation_failure and negative_failure assigns the heads; 2.0's output is close to affine in the fraction of open brackets.

cap.1: But the neat story isn't the whole model. Extra logic in layer 1, and heads helping outside their own jobs, make up the part it missed.
cap.2: Causal scrubbing of the combined story recovered about 72% of the loss. Some pathways or features the model uses aren't in the explanation.
cap.3: Both heads opportunistically vote on each other's failure class because log-loss rewards agreement, and layer-1 heads do logic the standard exercises don't cover.

cap.1: Here you know the right answer, so you can see exactly how good the explanation is. On a real model you'd never get this check.
cap.2: That's the point of the task: a calibration run for your tools, where findings, misses and inventions can all be counted.
cap.3: A method's recall on known mechanisms bounds how much to trust it where no ground truth exists.

predict.q: Why study a tiny model trained on balanced brackets instead of going straight to a big LLM?

options.t: The correct algorithm is known, so you can grade your explanation
Brackets are especially hard for language models

predict.why: Known ground truth turns interpretability into a measurement: you can check what your method found, missed or invented.

predict.q: Causal scrubbing of the combined two-heads story recovered about 72% of the loss. What does that tell you?

options.t: The story is incomplete: some pathways or features are missing

predict.why: Scrubbing resamples everything the story calls irrelevant. Losing 28% means some of that 'irrelevant' computation mattered.

predict.q: The string ') ( ) (' has equal numbers of opens and closes. Is it balanced?

options.t: No: scanning right to left, the count dips below zero
Only if you read it left to right

predict.why: Balance needs both clauses: end at zero and never go negative. This string fails the second, head 2.1's check.

object.where: Any known-answer test bench: planted bugs for code checkers, synthetic data for statistics, toy models for interpretability.
